doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Teaching masterclasses and practical studio advice
summary: He teaches master classes at Peabody, stresses practical habits like cable dressing and making artists comfortable, and recalls being told an engineer is one-third technician, musician and politician; Rowe cites Hank Cicalo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I do some courses, like master classes down at Peabody. I will bring down some SNL material and we’ll play that and we’ll talk about problems or listen to this leakage, listen to what we’re doing here; and then there’ve been other times when we’ve brought in some local musicians and they all know it’s kind of like these guys are going be actually watching us like this was an operating theater. But I’ll work with the class and we’ll set up and we’ll record like a small fusion jazz ensemble and okay well let’s try this, you want to put this bass here, drums there, okay, but you know there may be better issues as far — it may be better for the leakage but I’d rather work with the leakage and at least have the bass and the drummer be able to see each other. So to me it’s all of that real world stuff. This is going to be such a digression but someone was once telling me about her dad frying a turkey. And she said what he does is he’ll put the turkey in the empty big container, fill it with water, pull the turkey out and then measure the water, and then he knows that’s how much oil to use. Because so many people fill the thing up, they put the turkey in and it spills over, it hits the fire and then fighter jets scramble because of the heat plume. You think something’s launching. Now that kind of real-life common sense heads-up ball, that’s how I love to approach what we do. And also don’t lose sight of the music and don’t lost sight of make it as comfortable and as easy for these people to make music. I never want to be in a studio situation where the pianist is like well yeah if I do this I can see the bass player. They shouldn’t have to do that. And so which is why I’m always at sessions early making sure things are set up. The first thing, I’ll sit at the piano and be like yeah well, I mean do you need to see the ocarina and zither player or not? It’s all of this stuff. And that is what I don’t know how much of that is taught. So when you said about the real world, you know, in a classroom situation, I like to talk about let’s dress cables all in one direction around a drum kit and let’s be careful how we set up our drum mics. You know if you have a mic stand here, you know you have a mic stand, well don’t put the mic here, you bring things up and down like this so that no one walks around the far end and knocks things out of place. Well that was beaten, I’m sorry, drilled into me back in 1981 and it’s all of that practical stuff which I think is just so key. And at that very first job, and I still remember this and I still talk about it and this is 40 years ago I guess, where I was told when you are an engineer you are one-third technician, one-third musician, one-third politician. And you have to be all those things at once to everybody. And it’s just a huge help, and if you approach it that way — you know I like to make things easy-going. It doesn’t mean I’m not paying attention and watching meters and reels or computer screens like a hawk, but it should just be relaxed.
I’m so happy to hear you say that. I just did an interview not that long ago with a fellow named Hank Cicalo.

He said, more than once, that his main goal was always to make the artist comfortable. And you are echoing that. And the thing you said about the mic stand I think is very apropos because I’ve learned if you’re setting up in a tight situation to not have the end of the mic pole sticking out too far because someone’s going to hit it and the mic is going to end up in your teeth.
So your real-life experience is good.

You know you might find this with a lot of engineers, I love to cook. And my kids like to cook. And I’m always teaching them all the little bits of shortcuts and how to do this and what to do and think things through because it just makes your job that much easier.
